title: Fast Lanes
similar: LeetCode 2093 Minimum Cost to Reach City With Discounts
hints: Without express lanes this is plain shortest path. What extra fact about a position do you need once lanes exist?
Two visits to the same service are different situations if they have used a different number of lanes. Make that count part of the state.
Run Dijkstra over states (service, lanes used). A normal edge keeps the layer and adds w; an express edge moves to the next layer and adds 0. Answer: the best distance to service n over every layer.

wrong.greedy_waive.cpp: finds one shortest path, then waives its k heaviest edges (a different path can be better once lanes exist)
wrong.forget_layers.cpp: keeps one distance per service, so a cheap early arrival with lanes spent hides a pricier arrival with lanes in hand
wrong.int_overflow.cpp: stores distances in 32-bit ints, which overflow on long routes
wrong.tle_array_scan.cpp: Dijkstra that picks the next state by scanning every state (fails the perf group)

strategy.question: Scout the statement: services form a directed graph with latencies up to 10^9, and you may waive the latency of up to k <= 10 edges on your route. Which plan fits n up to 2*10^4?
options: Plain Dijkstra, then waive the k heaviest edges on the path it finds
Dijkstra on states (service, lanes used), so each layer is a copy of the graph
Try all subsets of k edges to waive and run Dijkstra for each
BFS by edge count, ignoring latencies
strategy.why: Waiving the heaviest edges of one fixed shortest path is a greedy that a different route can beat. Subsets of edges are far too many. BFS ignores weights. Layering the graph by 'lanes used' turns the problem into an ordinary shortest path on (k+1)n states with non-negative weights, which Dijkstra solves in O(k (n+m) log(kn)).
